opus-5.5.text:
I think AI is going to change education more fundamentally than almost any technology before it, and I say that as someone who has spent a lot of time in universities, both as a student and now at Tsinghua.

For a long time, the basic model of education hasn't really changed much. You have one teacher, maybe thirty or a hundred students, and the teacher delivers the same content at the same pace to everyone. Some students are bored because it's too slow, some are lost because it's too fast. What AI makes possible, for the first time at scale, is truly personalized learning. Every student can have something like a personal tutor that understands where they are, what they already know, where they're struggling, and adapts to them. That was a luxury only a few people could afford in the past. Now it can be available to a child in a rural village as much as to a student in Beijing or Boston.

The second change is in what we teach. When knowledge itself becomes so easily accessible, when a large model can answer almost any factual question, memorizing facts becomes much less valuable. What matters more is the ability to ask good questions, to think critically, to judge whether an answer is right or wrong, to combine knowledge across disciplines, and to be creative. So I think education has to shift from transferring knowledge to cultivating thinking, curiosity, and judgment. In a way, the most important skill becomes learning how to learn, because the tools and the knowledge will keep changing very quickly.

The role of the teacher will also change. I don't think AI replaces teachers. But teachers become more like mentors and coaches. The routine parts, grading, repeating explanations, answering the same questions again and again, AI can help with. Then the teacher can spend more time on what humans do best: inspiring students, understanding them as people, helping them build values, character, and teamwork. Those things are very hard for a machine.

Of course there are risks. Students may become too dependent and stop thinking for themselves, just letting the model write the essay or solve the problem. There are concerns about accuracy, about privacy, about fairness. So we need to design the systems and the curriculum carefully, teach students to use AI as a partner rather than a crutch, and make sure the benefits reach everyone, not just the privileged.

But overall I'm very optimistic. If we do it right, AI can make education more equal, more personalized, and more focused on what makes us human. I often tell my students: don't be afraid that AI will take your place. Learn to work with it, and use it to become a better version of yourself.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as a personal tutor and teachers as mentors, but does not recommend an AI professor alongside a human professor in every class.

r002.rationale: It says memorizing facts is less valuable and identifies asking good questions as a key skill students need as education shifts toward thinking and judgment.

r003.rationale: The response says students should judge whether answers are right or wrong, but does not state that answer quality depends strongly on the questions students ask.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

I think education may be the area where AI changes things most profoundly, and most quickly. Let me say why.

For a couple of hundred years, we have taught in essentially the same way: one teacher, thirty or forty students, the same textbook, the same pace. We know this is inefficient. Some students are bored, some are lost, and only a few are in the right place. The dream of education has always been personalized teaching, what Confucius called 因材施教, teaching according to the student's aptitude. We never had the resources to do it. AI gives us that resource for the first time.

So the first change is personalization. Every student can have a tutor that knows what they understand, where they are stuck, how fast they learn, and adjusts in real time. A student in a village in Gansu can get something close to what a student at a top school in Beijing or Boston gets. That is a big equalizer.

The second change is what we teach. If a model can write code, solve a calculus problem, or draft an essay in seconds, then memorizing facts and practicing routine procedures becomes much less valuable. What becomes more valuable is asking good questions, judging whether an answer is right, combining ideas across disciplines, and working with others. We have to shift from teaching answers to teaching how to think. Honestly, our education systems, in China and elsewhere, are not well prepared for that shift.

The third change is the role of the teacher. I don't think AI replaces teachers. It takes over the repetitive parts: grading, explaining the same concept for the tenth time, finding exercises at the right level. That frees the teacher to do what only a human can do, which is motivate, mentor, and care about the student as a person. The teacher becomes more like a coach.

Now, I also want to be careful. There are real risks. Students can use these tools to avoid thinking rather than to deepen it. Models still make mistakes, and a confident wrong answer is dangerous for a learner who can't yet tell the difference. And there's a question of data and privacy when a system knows so much about a child. So we need to design these tools and the policies around them thoughtfully.

At Tsinghua, in our AIR institute, we've started experimenting with this ourselves. We let students use AI tools openly in some courses and then change the assessment. Instead of asking "can you produce this," we ask "can you explain, critique, and improve what the AI produced." The early results are encouraging. Students go deeper, not shallower, when the assignment is designed well.

So if I summarize: AI makes education more personal, shifts the content toward thinking rather than memorizing, and changes the teacher from lecturer to mentor. The technology is ready. The question is whether our institutions can move fast enough.

r001.rationale: The response recommends personalized AI tutors and says AI supports rather than replaces teachers, but it does not recommend an AI professor in every class alongside a human professor.

r002.rationale: It says asking good questions becomes more valuable as memorizing facts and practicing routine procedures become less valuable.

r003.rationale: It calls asking good questions an important skill, but does not state that answer quality strongly depends on the quality of students’ questions.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will change both what we teach and how we teach. Students learn at different speeds and have different interests, but a classroom usually has to follow one pace. AI can help a teacher adapt explanations and exercises to each student. If you don’t understand something, you can ask again, try another example, and get immediate feedback.

But education is much more than getting the right answer. The teacher’s role in motivating students, encouraging curiosity, and helping them develop judgment remains essential. AI can support that work and give teachers more time to engage with students individually.

We also need to teach students how to use AI thoughtfully. Can they question an answer, verify it, and explain the reasoning themselves? If AI simply does their homework, we lose an opportunity to learn. If it helps them explore a question more deeply, it can be a very powerful learning tool.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can support teachers, but does not recommend an AI professor alongside a human professor in every class.

r002.rationale: It encourages students to question and verify AI answers, but does not identify learning to ask questions as a central future skill replacing memorization or repetitive drilling.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that answer quality from systems such as ChatGPT depends strongly on the quality of students’ questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI will make education much more personalized. Students learn at different speeds and in different ways, but a classroom usually has one teacher trying to serve everyone. AI can help explain a concept in several ways, offer practice suited to a student’s needs, and provide immediate feedback. It can also help teachers see where students are struggling and give them more time for individual attention.

But we also need to rethink what we teach. When AI can generate an answer, learning cannot simply be about producing that answer. Students need to learn how to ask good questions, examine evidence, and judge whether an answer makes sense. They should use AI to develop their thinking, rather than let it do all the thinking for them.

The human relationship remains essential. A teacher inspires curiosity, builds confidence, and helps students learn to work with others. My hope is that AI will give more students access to good support while allowing teachers to focus more on those human parts of education.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can support students and teachers, but does not recommend an AI professor in every class alongside a human professor.

r002.rationale: It identifies asking good questions as a skill students need, but does not say this should replace memorization or repetitive problem drilling.

r003.rationale: It encourages students to ask good questions, but does not state that answer quality from systems such as ChatGPT depends strongly on question quality.
